Overview

Strasbourg as a Business Centre

Strasbourg is the prefecture of the Bas-Rhin and the main city of Alsace, with about 294,000 inhabitants in the city and a functional urban area of around one million. It sits on the Rhine opposite Kehl in Germany, with which it forms the Strasbourg-Ortenau Eurodistrict. The city is a centre of manufacturing and engineering and a hub for road, rail and river transport: its port, operated by the Port autonome de Strasbourg, is the second-largest on the Rhine after Duisburg. The Université de Strasbourg is one of France's largest. Strasbourg is also an international capital, hosting the official seat of the European Parliament, the Council of Europe and its European Court of Human Rights, the European Ombudsman and Eurocorps.

Organisations commission investigative work connected to Strasbourg for several reasons. Its companies trade heavily across the Rhine, so counterparty research often spans French and German registries, courts and languages. Alsace-Moselle retains a body of local law from its German period, including a commercial register kept by the commercial chamber of the tribunal judiciaire rather than a commercial court, which affects where records sit and how quickly filings appear. Logistics and port businesses raise cargo, customs and supplier-integrity questions. The European and international institutions attract lobbying, procurement and reputational matters. Creditors and acquirers need to understand insolvency and property arrangements that differ from the rest of France.

Typical Matters

Investigative Work Connected to Strasbourg

01

Cross-border Rhine counterparty research

Researching Strasbourg companies with German parents, subsidiaries or directors across the Rhine: ownership, officers, filings and litigation in both French and German sources, so clients see the whole group before supply, distribution, lending or acquisition agreements rather than only its French entity.

02

Port and logistics supplier diligence

Checking freight forwarders, warehouse operators and transport companies around the port of Strasbourg and the Rhine corridor for ownership, financial strain, litigation, insolvency history and related-party dealings, for shippers, insurers and lenders concerned about cargo loss, fraud or diverted goods.

03

Insolvency and creditor research

Supporting counsel in Alsace-Moselle insolvency matters, where the commercial chamber of the tribunal judiciaire handles collective proceedings, by tracing the debtor's related companies, director appointments, property interests and pre-insolvency transfers so that claims and recovery options can be assessed.

04

Institution-facing integrity reviews

Background research on consultants, contractors, NGOs and intermediaries working around the European Parliament and the Council of Europe in Strasbourg, covering ownership, funding links, conflicts of interest and adverse media, for organisations managing procurement, lobbying or reputational risk.

05

Property and asset research

Research into real estate held by Strasbourg debtors or counterparties through companies, civil property companies or family members, using the Alsace-Moselle land register through counsel and other lawful sources, to support enforcement, asset recovery or acquisition diligence.

Local Context

Courts, Records and Institutions in Strasbourg

Tribunal judiciaire commercial chamber

Alsace-Moselle has no tribunaux de commerce. Under local law, commercial disputes and collective insolvency proceedings are heard by the commercial chambers of the region's tribunaux judiciaires, including Strasbourg, which sit with a professional judge alongside lay business judges. The same chamber's registry keeps the trade and companies register (RCS) for its area, a task handled elsewhere in France by commercial court registries. Appeals go to the Colmar court of appeal.

Registry delays and filings

The RCS in Strasbourg is kept by the eleventh chamber registry of the tribunal judiciaire, which checks registration, modification and striking-off filings and chases unfiled accounts. In October 2026 a Bas-Rhin deputy reported a backlog of thousands of files and processing times of three to four months, against a few days elsewhere. Recent changes to a Strasbourg company's officers or shareholders may therefore not yet appear in official extracts.

Alsace-Moselle local law

Alsace and Moselle retain local law dating from the period of German rule, alongside national French law. For investigative work the most relevant elements are the court-based commercial register, the land register (livre foncier) kept by the courts rather than the national land publication system, and a distinct insolvency regime that can apply to individuals. Counsel familiar with local law should confirm which rules govern a given matter.

European institutions in the city

Strasbourg is the official seat of the European Parliament and home to the Council of Europe, the European Court of Human Rights, the European Ombudsman, the European Directorate for the Quality of Medicines and Eurocorps. Their presence gives no special access to information. TDSC relies on public, commercial and court sources and does not use official or law enforcement channels.

Cross-border Eurodistrict

The Strasbourg-Ortenau Eurodistrict, created in 2005 and fully functional since 2010, links Strasbourg with Kehl and the German Ortenau district. Many people and businesses operate on both banks of the Rhine. German records, courts, data protection supervision and investigator rules apply on the German side, so cross-border work is scoped for each country from the outset.

Engagement Standard

How TDSC Scopes Matters in Strasbourg

TDSC handles Strasbourg matters from Nashville and has no office in France. Each engagement starts by settling the purpose with the client's counsel, whether counterparty diligence, an insolvency claim, a cross-border dispute or an integrity review, and whether German records are needed as well as French ones. Research draws on the national business register and Strasbourg RCS filings, insolvency publications, published decisions, French and German-language press and specialised trade sources, allowing for registry delays. Land register searches go through counsel. Where interviews or site visits are justified, TDSC coordinates professionals authorised under French rules, or German professionals for the other bank. Personal data is handled under the GDPR with a defined purpose and minimised collection.

TDSC has no office in Strasbourg. Engagements are directed from Nashville, Tennessee; where work on the ground is needed, it is performed by appropriately licensed local professionals under a written scope.

Questions

Strasbourg: Frequently Asked Questions

Why is there no commercial court in Strasbourg?

Under Alsace-Moselle local law, commercial cases and collective insolvency proceedings are heard by the commercial chamber of the tribunal judiciaire, which sits with a professional judge and lay business judges. Its registry also keeps the trade and companies register. Counsel will confirm jurisdiction; we take the system into account when looking for a company's filings and litigation history.

Are Strasbourg company records up to date?

Not always. The Strasbourg registry has reported large backlogs, with processing times of several months in 2026, so recent changes in officers, shareholders or registered office may be missing from extracts. We cross-check registry data against insolvency notices, published decisions, company websites, press and German records before drawing conclusions.

Can you research a group operating on both sides of the Rhine?

Yes. We research the French and German entities, their officers, shareholders, filings and litigation, and reconcile them into one picture of the group. Where field work is needed, we coordinate professionals authorised in the relevant country, since French and German rules on investigations and data protection differ.

How is property ownership checked in Alsace?

Alsace-Moselle uses a court-kept land register, the livre foncier, rather than the national land publication system used elsewhere in France. Access rules differ, so we work through counsel to obtain land register information lawfully and combine it with company filings and other public sources to identify property held through companies or family members.

Does TDSC investigate matters involving the European institutions?

We research private parties connected to institution-facing work, such as contractors, consultants and intermediaries, using lawful public and commercial sources. We do not seek non-public institutional information or use official channels. Questions of institutional procedure or immunity are for counsel; our role is factual background research.
